Why we decided to change the release cadence

answer.question: How many Kubernetes minor releases happen per year?
answer.answer: Kubernetes minor releases currently happen about three times per year (chunk 7600). The 1.22 changelog records that from April 23, 2021, the release cadence was officially reduced from 4 to 3 releases per year. The KEP that formalized this proposed 15-week release cycles. Some sources disagree. KEP-1498's motivation says minor releases come every 3 months, and KEP-2572's motivation says the project releases 4 times per year. Both describe the earlier cadence. They lose to the current tier-2 release documentation, which says roughly three releases per year.

answer.question: When was the move to three releases a year decided, and which release was the first to follow it?
answer.answer:
The move to three releases a year was made official on April 23, 2021, when the Release Team merged the KEP (KEP-2572) that changed the cycle from four releases a year to three. The 1.22 release notes and the release-cadence blog post both give this date.

The formal cadence was first applied to Kubernetes 1.22. The KEP says it would shape the release calendars for 1.22 and 1.23, each 15 weeks long.

In practice, three releases a year had already started on an ad hoc basis in 2020, beginning with Kubernetes 1.19. That cycle was extended because of the COVID-19 pandemic, and 1.20 became the third and final release of 2020.

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes move to three releases per year?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes formally moved from four to three releases per year when the Release Team merged KEP-2572 on April 23, 2021. The three-release cadence had in effect started ad hoc in 2020: the 1.19 cycle was extended because of the COVID-19 pandemic, and 1.20 became the third and final release of 2020. The KEP formalized that cadence.

The reasons given are:
- **Growing workload.** As the project matures, each cycle carries more enhancements. That adds work for contributors and the Release Engineering team, and makes it harder for downstream consumers and integrators to keep up with feature-packed releases.
- **Longer support.** Consumers get longer support terms per minor version, because the last three releases are supported. One release lead said this now covers a full calendar year instead of 9 of 12 months.
- **More time to mature enhancements.** Contributors get more time to mature enhancements and make them production-ready.
- **Less management overhead.** SIG Release and Release Engineering spend less on management, freeing time to improve release quality and tooling.
- **Predictability.** Fewer releases leave more room for triage, development, conferences and cycle preparation, giving better planning and a more deterministic schedule.
- **User feedback.** The release team listened to its user base about the number of releases per calendar year.

heading_path: Using the built-in Pod Security Admission Controller
The rise of Pod Security Admission

answer.question: What enforces pod security standards in-tree?
answer.answer:
The built-in Pod Security admission controller (Pod Security Admission, the `PodSecurity` admission plugin) enforces the Pod Security Standards in-tree. It applies restrictions at the namespace level, when pods are created. Namespaces opt into one of three policies, privileged, baseline or restricted, through labels. Policies can run in three modes:
- enforce: violations are rejected
- audit: violations get an audit annotation
- warn: violations produce a user-facing warning

You can also configure cluster-wide defaults and exemptions (by username, RuntimeClass or namespace). You do this with a PodSecurityConfiguration passed to kube-apiserver through `--admission-control-config-file`.

The controller was alpha in v1.22 and beta and on by default in v1.23. It has been stable since v1.25. It replaces the deprecated and since-removed PodSecurityPolicy, and it can be combined with admission webhooks or third-party solutions.

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes stop auto-generating Secret-based ServiceAccount tokens?
answer.answer: According to KEP-2799's motivation, BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume went GA in Kubernetes 1.22. From then on, Pods' service account tokens were obtained through the TokenRequest API and stored in a projected volume. That removed the need to auto-generate Secret-based service account tokens, which are less secure than bound tokens (chunk 16052). The docs and the v1.29 blog describe the more secure tokens the same way: they are time-limited, bound to specific Pods, and automatically invalidated when the Pod is deleted (chunks 6095, 43086). Auto-generation was stopped in 1.24, when the LegacyServiceAccountTokenNoAutoGeneration feature gate became beta and enabled by default (chunks 11774, 43086). Users are pointed to the TokenRequest API instead, or can manually create a Secret if they need a non-expiring token (chunks 11774, 6095).

answer.question: Does the API server reject IP addresses with leading zeros by default?
answer.answer: Yes, as of Kubernetes 1.36 and later. The StrictIPCIDRValidation feature gate moved to beta in 1.36 and is enabled by default (it was alpha and disabled by default in 1.33–1.35). With it enabled, octets in IPv4 addresses may not have leading 0s, and IPv4-mapped IPv6 values such as ::ffff:192.168.0.1 are forbidden. The 1.36 changelog says API fields no longer allow IP or CIDR values with extraneous leading 0s (e.g. 010.000.000.005), or CIDR values with ambiguous semantics. This stricter validation applies only to fields in built-in API kinds. It does not apply to custom resources, Kubernetes configuration files or command-line arguments. In 1.33–1.35, with the gate disabled by default, such values were accepted, but the API server returned a warning that they will be rejected in the future. Earlier still, the 1.23 changelog states that Kubernetes kept allowing leading zeros on IPv4 addresses for compatibility, interpreting them as decimal.

answer.question: What are the release stages of strict IP/CIDR validation (KEP-4858)?
answer.answer:
Strict IP/CIDR validation (feature gate StrictIPCIDRValidation, KEP-4858) went through these stages:
- Alpha from Kubernetes v1.33 through v1.35, disabled by default. The KEP's alpha criteria say the updated validation was available behind a feature gate but off by default.
- Beta from v1.36, enabled by default. The KEP's implementation history also records "Alpha in Kubernetes v1.33" and "Beta in Kubernetes v1.36".

The latest KEP text claims implemented/stable with a latest milestone of v1.38. The feature-gate reference still shows beta (observed at 1.37), and no GA stage appears in the gate documentation. So the observed stage is beta; the code-detected conflict resolves in favour of the observed stage over the KEP's claim.

When enabled, the gate forbids leading zeros in IPv4 octets and IPv4-mapped IPv6 values. This applies only to fields in built-in API kinds.

heading_path: Changes to supported skew between control plane and node versions

answer.question: Before v1.28, how many minor versions older than kube-apiserver could the kubelet be?
answer.answer: Before v1.28, the kubelet could be at most two minor versions older than kube-apiserver, and it could never be newer than it. In an HA cluster where the kube-apiserver instances are at different versions, the allowed kubelet range narrows: for example, with kube-apiserver instances at N and N-1, the kubelet was supported only at N-1 and N-2. Starting with v1.28 the policy allows up to three minor versions older (kubelets older than 1.25 are still limited to two). Older and newer versions of the same policy page say this. The v1.28 release blog says the same thing: the skew was widened from n-2 to n-3.

answer.question: In Kubernetes 1.20, how did you turn on IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack networking?
answer.answer:
In 1.20 dual-stack was still alpha and off by default, so you had to switch it on yourself. You enabled the `IPv6DualStack` feature gate on the relevant components and set dual-stack (IPv4,IPv6) network ranges:
- kube-apiserver: `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"` and `--service-cluster-ip-range=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`.
- kube-controller-manager: `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"`, `--cluster-cidr=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>` and `--service-cluster-ip-range=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`. Per-node mask sizes come from `--node-cidr-mask-size-ipv4|--node-cidr-mask-size-ipv6`, which default to /24 for IPv4 and /64 for IPv6.
- kubelet: `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"`.
- kube-proxy: `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"` and `--cluster-cidr=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`.

Prerequisites were Kubernetes 1.20 or later, provider support for routable IPv4/IPv6 node interfaces, and a network plugin that supports dual-stack (such as Kubenet or Calico). In 1.20 dual-stack was reimplemented so that, once enabled, Services could use IPv4, IPv6, or both, and existing Services could be changed. From 1.21 onward the gate went to beta and was on by default, so this explicit enablement applies to 1.20 specifically.
